direct_answer: Not drinking enough can raise the risk of gout attacks and cause other problems in frailty, such as confusion, constipation and falls. Drinking regularly, eating well and taking gout medicines as prescribed help. Some medicines and conditions need fluid advice from your GP.

content:
Gout is a type of arthritis caused by urate crystals in the joints. Older people are more likely to become dehydrated, which can make gout attacks more likely.

This guide explains how hydration fits into gout care. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why hydration matters

  • Dehydration can contribute to gout attacks.
  • It can also cause dizziness, confusion and constipation.
  • Thirst can be weaker in older age.

Practical ways to drink more

  • Keep a drink within reach.
  • Use cups that are easy to hold.
  • Drink regularly through the day.
  • Foods such as soup and fruit add fluid.
  • Ask your GP if you have been told to limit fluids.

Food, fluid and muscle when gout shrinks cooking

During an attack, cooking can be hard. Keep simple, nourishing foods available. Eating enough protein helps keep muscles strong. Limit sugary drinks and alcohol, especially beer.

Treatment

Medicines can treat attacks and lower urate levels to prevent them. Keep taking prescribed urate-lowering medicine during an attack unless told otherwise.

When to get help

  • Call 999 if someone is collapsed or very drowsy.
  • Get urgent advice from NHS 111 or your GP if a hot, swollen joint comes with fever or feeling unwell, as this may be a joint infection.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Should I stop allopurinol during a flare?

No, unless your doctor advises it.

Does water prevent gout?

Drinking enough may help reduce attacks, alongside treatment.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Gout
  • NHS: Malnutrition
